content:
AI is producing novel math results at a increasing rate and of increasing importance. Lean has solidified itself as the first pass on correctness of such results. With autoformalization it seems to be reasonable to expect that most novel result to come with a lean certificate. With https://palomar-registry.org/ there is a clear expectation how should such formalization repo look like. However, the next step is human digestion (per Tao's terminology) of the result and it is the arguably the hardest and slowest step and we have the least of shared understanding and community suggestions on how to structure and help that part.

I am curious to have a thread where folks can share:

  • if you have done such a digestion, what has helped and what was not useful. Some possible strategies
    • asking AI to produce a classical informal paper and just read that
    • staying close to the lean files and navigating those in and IDE and clicking around. Hopefully the proofs have good comments.
    • conversation with an AI that points to different parts of the autoformalization until the whole think clicks.
  • do folks see divergences between the digestion companion and the lean proof? There is a tradeoff, where the further one gets from the lean proof, hypothetically the nicer the digestion artefact could be, but more of the correctness guarantees could be lost.
  • what affordances would one ask autoformalized results to have that would make other folks more likely to spend their valuable time digesting the reuslt. We are having the situation where is it somewhat cheap for autoformalizers to produce such artifacts, but it is not very clear which ones are actually of help (or even looked at). Some examples I have seen:
    • https://mattrobball.github.io/BridgelandStability/
    • https://mazur-theorem-formalization.vilin402100.chatgpt.site/
    • https://www.math.cmu.edu/~wes/trellis/spgt-viewer/
  • would it make sense for a community best practice for a digestion helper?

One example of digestion being hard is Akhil Mathew's AI-generated example of a group scheme of order 4 which is not killed by 4. I talked to him about this last week and neither he nor anyone else seems to have a conceptual understanding of what is going on. This is a very short argument (under 1000 lines in Counterexamples in mathlib) but right now is just "here's some algebra and it works out".

That's a good reminder that sometimes digestion means much more than navigating through a large lean proof (which what I was thinking about), but one has to ask for missing insights. I guess https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/07/21/a-digestion-of-the-jacobian-conjecture-counterexample/ is another example where a very short lean proof needed to be pulled apart to understand why it works.

For me, asking to make a list of 1-1 correspondence between informal paper (if exists) and formal proof was very helpful. Although this is usually not perfect, LLMs can at least give a list and then human can start to check from there, which is much more efficient then starting from scratch with enormous Lean code. If there's no separate informal paper, then one can simply ask to make blueprint from Lean code. Sometimes you can also find that formal proof is "different" from existing informal proof. (Basically, I was just using LLM as search engine with two documents)
For digestion itself (which may have nothing to do with formal proofs), it was helpful to read line by line and asking for intuitions behind proofs. In my experience, without any further guidance, LLMs tend to answer by almost copy-pasting sentences from the paper, which was not helpful. So I explicitly added something like "do not simply repeat phrases in the paper - give other explanations" to prompt and the answers were better in my opinion.

For a civilization, digestion of AI output on open problems may have a higher cost than its worth due to its low signal-to-noise ratio (taking the agent/model cost into account, not subsidized subscription price), and its effects of lock-in and path dependency.

Some people that are pro-digestion have raised an interesting metaphor: math is now back to pre-Newton, or pre-Galileo, and the job of mathematicians are to observe the trajectories of celestial bodies (a metaphor of AI with superior mathematical capabilities in the near future), and make sense of them with various ansatzes.

Some people that are anti-digestion believe that AI output fall into the convex hull of human intellectual work, and are incapable to breed genuine novel ideas.

Being an embrace-digestion person, I find it burning prohibitive amount of my braincells to digest AI output (formal and informal), even when the output was based on my heavy steering, and I'd familiarized myself with the math background in the old-fashion way. The work is much more than some reverse engineering of well specified binary format, but comparable to theorizing clueless experiment data.

I have some general thoughts on digestion that may or may not be helpful. I suspect that in many cases, the road to conceptual understanding involves a lot more than dissecting the proof itself. Instead, I think we have to ask "theory-building" questions. Does the result generalize? Does the proof generalize? How far does it generalize and what exactly is the obstacle to further generalization? Can the hypothesis be weakened? Can the conclusion be strengthened? Is the argument related to some other arguments that have been used in the literature in other contexts? Can we find other proofs of the same result? Or if the result has a "counterexample" flavor, what other counterexamples are there? Can we classify all counterexamples? Traditionally, getting anwers to these questions might take a lot of time and effort, but nowadays, that process can often be accelerated.

I should add at least one more question to my above list. Why do simpler arguments not work? Failed proofs can often give conceptual insight; we can overlook this fact if we overemphasize only correct proofs.

Building on Timothy's post above, I think a good digestion should open doors for more research in the future.

A good math paper is not just one that closes the door on an open question--but rather one that expands the horizons to see how much further we can push our techniques and understanding.

Digesting why failed proofs don't work (and possibly identifying future research areas from them, etc.) generally requires access to the failed ideas in the first place, which often aren't exposed for AI-generated proofs (this is a way in which an AI-generated solution can damage progress, as discussed by Tao, because future work will be biased by knowing what approach worked, and humans would probably have generated lots of papers based on attempts along the way even where those attempts didn't end up contributing to the solution of the problem).

Humans also often "conceal" failed proofs in the sense of not publishing them. I think it's important to distinguish how a proof (or a failed proof) was originally generated from a nice story about how it might have been generated. One might think that true stories are necessarily better than made-up stories, but I don't think that's necessarily the case. If someone asks me how I came up with a proof, the truly honest answer is that I have no idea. Nobody knows how human brain works, and I certainly don't know how my brain actually works. Instead, I answer the question by telling a story, which contains some elements of truth, but more importantly, it's supposed to give other people some clues as to how they might find proofs of other, related results. A literally correct answer that provides millions of MRI images of my brain is useless, and not what people want.

Similarly, when people claim to want to know how an AI generated a proof, I don't believe that they want the true answer. The true answer is some incomprehensible kajillion-byte computational trace. What people are really saying is, "Tell me a story." As long as it's a good story, that has some elements of truth, but more importantly fosters understanding and is useful, it can be invented ex post facto. (Neurologists tell us that our brains are constantly inventing ex post facto stories.)

Similarly, to generate a failed proof, it is not necessary to capture the historical record of someone actually trying to prove something and failing. A "simulation" will do just fine, and may do even better. Even after you know a correct proof, try to prove it some other way, and figure out why it doesn't work.

Let me also suggest that part of the skill of theory-building is to ask precisely such "dumb questions." Never mind AI. If there is a well-known theorem with a well-known proof, most people will just take it as a given, and it will limit their thinking and imagination. The skilled theory-builder, on the other hand, will appear to not understand what others find obvious, and ask questions that others don't ask, because they sound pointless. I have previously elaborated on this point on MathOverflow.

Humans do at least sometimes publish (or pass ideas on to collaborators, etc.) partial progress on problems they didn't solve, or work that seemed interesting in its own right that arose out of such a failed attempt, or ideas for new problems arising from such attempts. I fully expect AI could extract such interesting pieces from the other directions it attempted if asked to do so, but "here are some interesting ideas and new problems to work on" doesn't make for a good press release the same way as "we solved this famous problem" does.

(Here an AI that solves a problem can be taking the place of several mathematicians over many years, each publishing partial progress until eventually the problem is solved; no doubt the "failed" approaches are more likely to be published in such a case than when it's all one mathematician who does all the work and solves the problem.)
Something akin to what I said above about failed proofs and made-up stories can be found in the paragraph about "discovery fiction" in Grant Sanderson's guest post on Terry Tao's blog.

The true answer is some incomprehensible kajillion-byte computational trace. What people are really saying is, "Tell me a story."

I'm not sure I agree that the true answer is necessarily "incomprehensible". Proof trajectories contain a lot of fascinating information. Even if the reasoning trace has been redacted by a proprietary LLM provider, the LLM can annotate the changes it has made to try to make progress as an approximation of the reasoning behind each change. I would have to do a lot of work to maintain equally detailed traces when I construct a proof, and so I don't bother.

It is possible to summarise the narrative of progress from proof trajectories, and my hope is that this is going to be useful and perhaps more truthful than the verisimilitude of narratives I tend to tell about my own work. It might not be interesting (maybe it was all just "try some obvious things until it works", cranked up to some huge multiple of human effort) but I think a story can be told. Moreover, unlike stories reported by humans, we can then go back and verify how well the story matches what actually happened, whether it succeeded or failed. I've also learned a lot of surprising things about problems I care about through the sequence of failed attempts tried by an LLM.

I agree that sometimes we can extract some interesting stories by examining the chain of thought. And perhaps we can also extract some interesting stories from MRIs taken while people think about mathematics. Still, I want to emphasize that it's stories that people actually want, even though they say they want to know how the person or AI came up with the proof. If we become overly fixated on the literal interpretation of the question, "How did you come up with that?" then that can lead us down the wrong path.
